cards.title: Design movements
cards.body: Arts and Crafts (late 1800s, William Morris): handcraft over machines. Art Nouveau: flowing natural curves. Bauhaus (Germany, 1919–1933): form follows function, unity of art and industry. Art Deco: geometric glamour. Swiss (International) Style: grids, sans-serif type, clarity. Memphis (1980s, Ettore Sottsass): playful colours and shapes. Minimalism: less, but better.

cards.title: Famous designers
cards.body: Dieter Rams (Braun): 'less, but better' and the ten principles of good design. Charles & Ray Eames: plywood and fibreglass chairs, and the India Report. Paul Rand: IBM and ABC logos. Milton Glaser: the 'I ♥ NY' logo. Massimo Vignelli: the New York subway map. Zaha Hadid: flowing architecture. Naoto Fukasawa: products that fit natural behaviour.

cards.title: Iconic products
cards.body: Products studied as design classics include the Eames Lounge Chair, the Braun SK4 radio, the Anglepoise lamp, the Swiss Army knife, the Coca-Cola contour bottle, the original iPod, the monobloc plastic chair (cheap, stackable, everywhere) and the bicycle. Ask what problem each solved and why it lasted.

cards.title: Sustainability & circular design
cards.body: A linear economy goes make → use → throw. A circular economy keeps materials in use: design for durability, repair, reuse, remanufacture and recycling, and use renewable materials. Life-cycle thinking considers raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and end of life. Many traditional Indian practices (repair, reuse, leaf plates) are already circular.

cards.title: Universal & inclusive design
cards.body: Universal design makes things usable by as many people as possible without special adaptation: ramps, lever handles, large text, low-floor buses. Inclusive design also considers age, language, culture and situational limits (carrying shopping, a broken arm). Key principles: equitable use, flexibility, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low effort, and appropriate size and space.

cards.title: AI & emerging tech in design
cards.body: AI tools can generate images, text and layouts quickly, which is useful for exploration. But designers still define problems, understand users, judge quality and take responsibility. Other emerging areas: 3D printing (rapid prototyping), AR/VR, smart and connected products, and new bio-based materials. Ethics matters: privacy, bias and energy use.
